IDAHO’S STUDENT GROWTH
 TRAJECTORY MODEL

 Damian W Betebenner
 National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
 Boise, ID March 6th, 2018

BACKGROUND
• Idaho’s new vision for accountability is sharing clear, understandable
 data about school performance using a variety of indicators
 • Outlined in IDAPA Rule 08.02.03.112. We have provided a copy of this in your
 TAC materials.

• The state plans to make this information available via a new online
 Report Card

BACKGROUND
• For reporting, and identification, schools will be separated into three
 categories:
 • K-8 schools
 • High Schools
 • Alternative High Schools

• Each category of schools will have their own set of academic and
 school quality measures

BACKGROUND
• Idaho Code outlines the required measures, but with limited detail
• For example, the K-8 reporting must include “ISAT growth toward
 proficiency based on a trajectory model approved by the State Board
 of Education”
• There are several ways in which we could design a “trajectory” model.

THE TRAJECTORY MODEL
• Trajectory model is a broad term that could encompass several
 different types of “growth to standard” approaches.
• In some instances, student trajectories are based upon:
 • Predicted future outcome(s): Is the student predicted to reach the desired
 standard.
 • Desired future outcome(s): Is the student making annual progress sufficient to
 reach the desired standard.
• Based on previous conversations with the Board’s Accountability
 Oversight Committee, our understanding is that the Board is
 interested in the following type of model…

THE TRAJECTORY MODEL
• This model is conceptually straightforward

• Additionally, the model is consistent with the Idaho Standards
 Achievement Tests (ISATs) in ELA and Math scoring structure
 • Scale is vertically aligned and ranges from roughly 2,000 to 3,000

THE TRAJECTORY MODEL
• However, we still need to determine:
 • What standard is the student expected to reach?
 • Over what time period?
 • Using what growth assumption?

WHAT STANDARD IS THE STUDENT
 EXPECTED TO REACH?
• The ISAT has four performance levels: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, and
 Level 4

• Informally, these levels are interpreted as representing: Below Basic,
 Basic, Proficient, and Advanced performance

• Consequently, we have interpreted Idaho Code’s reference to “future
 proficiency” as using the Level 3 cut score
 • These scores are illustrated on the next slide

WHAT STANDARD IS THE STUDENT
 EXPECTED TO REACH?
• Potential considerations
 • Internally consistent with other measures of school achievement (e.g.
 proficiency rate), but also contains the same limitations as the proficiency
 calculation, such as creating a binary distinction between scores that are
 statistically equivalent (e.g. one point below and one point above the cut
 score). This results in a loss of information.
 • Potentially too ambitious for low achieving students.

OVER WHAT TIME PERIOD?
• Regardless of the target the state adopts, we also need to determine
 the time period over which a student is expected to reach that
 threshold

• For example, should a student be expected to reach this target over a
 set number of years (e.g. three years) or by a consistent end point
 (e.g. 8th grade)
 • And for either of these approaches, we would still need to make specific
 decisions about the number of years or end point to use

OVER WHAT TIME PERIOD?
• Idaho Code offers less guidance on this question than the it does for
 the growth standard

• Internally, conversations have generally focused on reaching the target
 by 8th grade
 • However, this was for simplicity and we have not addressed this issue in detail

OVER WHAT TIME PERIOD?
• Potential considerations
 • A set target, such as 8th grade, is easier to communicate because of its
 consistency but is generally more forgiving to students at earlier grades
 • In most growth to standard implementations, time frame has been 3 years or
 by the final grade, whichever came first. The desire for a fixed time frame was
 due to a desire to not provide too long a time frame so that schools “pass the
 buck”.
 • As a point of comparison. Many ELP testing programs use growth-to-standard.
 5 year time frame is typical but empirically derived.

USING WHAT GROWTH ASSUMPTION?
• Even with a growth target and timeframe in place, Idaho would need to determine
 how to establish future achievement targets (annual achievement targets can be
 converted to growth targets via simple subtraction).

• Generally, trajectory models base future achievement targets in two ways:
 • Predicted future outcome(s): Based upon linear trajectory assumptions or regression.
 • Desired future outcome(s): Based upon a trajectory leading toward proficiency.

• However, even within that framework, there are additional details we would need to
 address:
 • Does a student’s “historical growth” mean last year’s growth, the student’s average growth, a
 weighted composite of all past growth?
 • Should that growth be projected forward using linear growth assumptions or with
 adjustments for the “expected” scale score growth at different grade levels?

USING WHAT GROWTH ASSUMPTION?
• This topic is again something Idaho Code does not address in any
 detail

• Internal discussions have tended to focus on a student’s growth over
 the past year, with a linear projection forward
 • For example, if a student’s ELA scale score went up 25 points from Grade 3 to
 Grade 4, the accountability targets would establish a scale score increase by 25
 points each year in the future.
 • This is the projection seen in the Castellano and Ho chart
 • This trajectory might not lead to proficiency.

USING WHAT GROWTH TRAJECTORY
 ASSUMPTIONS?
• Potential considerations
 • Castellano and Ho state the linear projections in their trajectory model
 example are “not empirical as much as descriptive and aspirational.”
 • In fact, they categorize more refined, regression-based projection models separately from
 the trajectory approach
 • Increasing accuracy may result in more complicated calculations that are less
 understandable
 • Regardless of the approach, scale score targets are established that are used
 for determining whether progress is (un)satisfactory.

INVESTIGATION OF SUMMARY RESULTS
• Assuming achievement targets are established leading to proficiency
 in (i) 3 years or (ii) 8th grade, calculations with 2017 data were
 performed.
• Individual level results
• School level results

SUMMARY OF INDIVIDUAL LEVEL RESULTS
• Growth-to-Standard results show:
 • ELA: 55.3% of students reaching 3 year targets, 56.7% of students reaching 8th
 grade targets, and 57.1% reaching 10th grade targets.
 • Mathematics: 47.3% of students reaching 3 year targets, 49.3% of students
 reaching 8th grade targets, and 46.1% reaching 10th grade targets.
• More time increases chances of reaching the proficiency target. 7th
 grade students have only until either grade 8 or 10 to reach the target
 (1 or 2 time periods)
• Low achieving students have much more difficult targets to reach than
 higher achieving students.
• Economically disadvantaged students (who tend to be lower achieving
 than their non-disadvantaged counterparts) have more difficult targets.
• Special education students have more difficult targets as well.

SCHOOL LEVEL RESULTS
• Used for school level accountability, several summary statistics are
 available to examine probable impact including.
 • Correlation between percent meeting target and mean prior achievement
 • Correlation between percent economically disadvantaged and percent
 meeting target.
 • Correlation between percent special education and percent meeting target.

SUMMARY OF SCHOOL LEVEL RESULTS
• Growth-to-Standard results show:
 • Correlation between percent of students reaching growth target and prior
 achievement is strong. This is true regardless of whether 3 year, 8th grade, or
 10th grade is used and regardless of whether mean standardized prior
 achievement of percent proficient prior is used.
 • When broken out by content area, school level correlations remain strong.
 • Strong correlations between prior achievement and growth indicate that high
 achieving schools will mostly be flagged for high growth. This is generally a
 problematic finding.
 • Moderate to low correlations exist between percent of student reaching
 growth target and percent economically disadvantaged.
 • Moderate to low correlations exist between percent of student reaching
 growth target and percent special education.
• Results (particularly with prior achievement) are consistent with what
 is found in other states.
